takes.text: Tonight, a storm hits this harbour on a king tide. We start that morning.

This is Port Alder, a simulated harbour district running against a live DeviceChain instance. Forty-three devices report to one platform: tide gauges, storm pumps, street lights, vehicle chargers, power meters and a works truck.

This is Port Alder, a simulated harbour district running against a live DeviceChain instance. Its devices report to one platform: tide gauges, storm pumps, street lights, vehicle chargers, power meters and a works truck.
Its operators don't watch every reading. They write rules, and the platform carries them out and keeps the record. This is one day of that.
Mid-morning, the ferry terminal draws more power than its cap allows. The rule here watches a one-minute average, so a brief spike is ignored and only a sustained overdraw raises an alarm.
Mid-morning, the ferry terminal's meter climbs toward its power cap.
On East Quay a crew is servicing one street light, under a maintenance window its operators set.
On East Quay a crew is servicing one street light.
While they work, the light starts to flicker.
The platform still detects the fault, and marks it as raised during maintenance. A second lamp, with no window, flickers too, and its notification goes out at once.
The platform still detects the fault, and marks it as raised during maintenance.
The platform detects the fault.
The crew is still at the lamp.
The work ends and the window closes, but the fault is still there. Now the held notification goes out to the crew.
The work ends and the maintenance window closes.
At midday, one tide gauge gets new hardware. A crew swaps the unit, and the platform records the replacement.
At midday, one tide gauge gets new hardware. A crew swaps the unit on the quay wall.
On the platform it is still the same device: one unbroken line of tide readings.
The new unit takes over the old one's place on the wall.
And the old unit's credentials are disabled, so the retired hardware can no longer sign in.
The old unit is retired from the quay.
Mid-afternoon, a charger's connector runs hot. The platform raises an alarm and tells that charger to derate to eleven kilowatts.

The charger confirms the new limit. The connector cools, and the alarm clears.

Then the weather turns. By evening a storm is pushing a king tide into the harbour, and the rules written in daylight are about to be tested.
The works truck heads out from the depot.
Under North Quay, a storm drain is filling. The pump's own sensor reports the level in its well.
Under North Quay sits a storm drain, and the pump that empties it.

The water crosses the level the operators set. The platform raises an alarm and sends the pump a start command, and the pump confirms. It is running before its own float switch, the last line of defence, would have started it.
The water crosses the level the operators set. The platform raises an alarm and sends the pump a start command, and the pump confirms.
The well keeps rising toward the pump's own float switch, its last line of defence.
The outfall runs, the well drains into the harbour, and the alarm clears.
The pump empties the well into the harbour.
Along the quays, each tide gauge gets its own flood alarm, and it escalates in place as the water climbs.
Along the quays, the tide gauges follow the water as it climbs.
The works truck drives into the flood plain. A geofence rule records the moment it crosses the line, so the operators know where the crew is.
The works truck drives into the flood plain.
On East Quay, a second pump is running but moving no water. No single reading shows that. A rule that watches both, over time, raises a critical alarm, and a notification goes out.

Then the storm cuts power to East Quay. Its street lights and chargers go dark, and they stop reporting.
A device that has gone quiet cannot raise its own alarm. So the platform does it for them: it notices the silence and raises the alarms.
A device that has gone quiet cannot raise its own alarm.
Six silent devices, six alarms, six notifications sent.
The alarms are raised, and the notifications are sent.
The quay stays dark while the storm passes over.
When power returns, the chargers send everything they saved in the dark.

That is a burst, all at once. The platform asks them to slow down, and they retry. Each reading is stored at the moment it was taken, not when it arrived, so the gap in the record fills from left to right, until every buffered reading is in place.

The silence alarms clear as the devices report again.
East Quay is lit again.
The truck leaves the flood plain; that alarm clears too.
The truck heads back toward the depot.
